questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has a 6 day history of severe sore throat, fever, headache and exhaustion. Her boyfriend had glandular symptoms a month ago. She has enlarged tonsils with white exudate, petechiae on the palate and tender lymph nodes behind the sternocleidomastoid. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Glandular fever is EBV infection spread by saliva, with severe sore throat, fatigue, fever, exudative tonsils, palatal petechiae and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Teenager, saliva contact, exudative tonsillitis, palatal petechiae, posterior nodes, fatigue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever).

elim: Can cause a mononucleosis-like illness, but usually with a rash and mouth ulcers after a risk exposure.
Gives a mononucleosis-like illness with less prominent sore throat and exudate.
Unilateral swelling with uvular deviation and trismus.
Gives anterior, not posterior, cervical nodes and less fatigue.

steps.x: **C. Infectious mononucleosis.** Sore throat + fatigue + posterior cervical nodes + palatal petechiae in a teenager = glandular fever.

questions.stem: A 19 year old university student has had a sore throat, fever and severe tiredness for 8 days. She has been sleeping 14 hours a day. Her pharynx is red with enlarged tonsils. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her GP examines her neck carefully.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the neck?
questions.e: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is a key examination finding in infectious mononucleosis, alongside exudative tonsils, splenomegaly and palatal petechiae.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: sore throat, fever and severe tiredness for 8 days
steps.x: Sore throat with marked fatigue in a young adult.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

elim: Seen in mumps.
A thyroid swelling, not part of this illness.
Suggests an abscess.
Suggests quinsy, with a deviated uvula.

steps.x: **C. Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.** Glandular fever: posterior cervical nodes; bacterial tonsillitis: anterior cervical nodes.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has had a sore throat, fever and fatigue for 5 days. He has posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen tip. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. The doctor looks carefully inside his mouth with a torch for a finding that supports her suspected diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding in the mouth?
o: Unilateral tonsillar swelling with a deviated uvula
questions.e: Palatal petechiae, exudative tonsils and an inflamed pharynx are typical of infectious mononucleosis; Koplik spots and strawberry tongue belong to measles and scarlet fever.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Posterior nodes and splenomegaly with sore throat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palatal petechiae.

elim: White spots on the buccal mucosa in measles.
Primary herpes simplex gingivostomatitis.
Seen in scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease.
Quinsy.

steps.x: **C. Petechiae on the soft palate.** Palatal petechiae + posterior nodes + splenomegaly = glandular fever.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man is recovering from glandular fever. His dentist notices white, corrugated, 'hairy' plaques on the lateral borders of his tongue that cannot be scraped off. He has no pain. He has no risk factors for HIV and a recent HIV test was negative. He takes no inhalers or antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of this lesion?
questions.e: Oral hairy leucoplakia, a hairy white lesion on the lateral tongue, is caused by EBV and may be seen in infectious mononucleosis; candida plaques scrape off.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 'hairy' plaques on the lateral borders of his tongue
steps.x: Non-removable hairy white plaques on the lateral tongue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral hairy leucoplakia from EBV.

elim: Plaques can be scraped off, leaving a red base.
Causes painful vesicles and ulcers.
Causes warty papillomas, not hairy plaques on the tongue sides.
Causes glossitis and angular stomatitis.

steps.x: **B. Epstein-Barr virus.** Oral hairy leucoplakia = EBV; it cannot be scraped off, unlike candida.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman was diagnosed with glandular fever 2 weeks ago. Yesterday she lifted heavy boxes while moving house. She now has left upper abdominal pain and pain at the tip of her left shoulder that is worse lying down. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Her shoulder moves fully without pain.
questions.q: Which best explains her shoulder pain?
questions.e: Splenic rupture causes blood under the left diaphragm, giving referred left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign), with tachycardia and peritonism.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: pain at the tip of her left shoulder
steps.x: Recent glandular fever, straining, left upper abdominal and shoulder-tip pain, tachycardia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Kehr's sign from splenic rupture.

elim: Her shoulder moves fully without pain.
Gives arm pain with neck symptoms, not abdominal pain and tachycardia.
Very unlikely at 19 with abdominal pain after straining.
Would limit shoulder movement.

steps.x: **C. Diaphragmatic irritation from splenic rupture.** Glandular fever + left shoulder-tip pain + tachycardia = splenic rupture (Kehr's sign).

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has had glandular fever for 10 days with fever, sore throat and fatigue. He now has a dull ache under his right ribs and his urine is slightly darker. He drinks little alcohol and takes only paracetamol in normal doses. His sclerae are not obviously yellow. Liver blood tests are sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on liver blood tests?
o: ALT raised with raised inflammatory markers
Isolated raised ALP with dilated ducts
Very high ammonia with prolonged INR
questions.e: EBV commonly causes a mild viral hepatitis with deranged LFTs and raised inflammatory markers; acute liver failure is rare.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: dull ache under his right ribs
steps.x: EBV with right upper quadrant ache and darker urine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: EBV hepatitis: deranged LFTs with raised inflammatory markers.

elim: Suggests biliary obstruction.
Suggests Gilbert's syndrome or haemolysis.
His symptoms suggest liver involvement.
Suggests acute liver failure, which is rare in EBV.

steps.x: **A. ALT raised with raised inflammatory markers.** EBV hepatitis: deranged LFTs (raised transaminases) and raised inflammatory markers.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl with glandular fever is brought to the emergency department because her breathing has become noisy. Her tonsils are massively enlarged and almost touching in the midline. She is sitting upright, drooling and cannot swallow her saliva. Her oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on listening to her breathing?
questions.e: Massive tonsillar enlargement (or quinsy) in glandular fever can obstruct the upper airway, causing inspiratory stridor; wheeze reflects lower airway narrowing.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: drooling and cannot swallow her saliva
steps.x: Huge tonsils, drooling, noisy breathing: upper airway narrowing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inspiratory stridor.

elim: Seen in pulmonary oedema or fibrosis.
Suggests consolidation.
Pleuritic inflammation.
Lower airway narrowing, as in asthma.

steps.x: **B. Inspiratory stridor.** Upper airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement = inspiratory stridor: an emergency.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man has confirmed glandular fever. He asks how he caught it. He has not travelled, has no pets and has not had a blood transfusion or injected drugs. He started a new relationship 6 weeks ago and his partner had a sore throat and fatigue 2 months ago.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of transmission?
questions.e: Infectious mononucleosis is EBV infection transmitted via saliva, hence 'the kissing disease'.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: partner had a sore throat and fatigue
steps.x: Close contact with an unwell new partner.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Saliva (kissing).

elim: He has had none.
Not a route for EBV.
The route for hepatitis A, not EBV.
Spreads malaria and dengue, not EBV.

steps.x: **E. Saliva.** EBV spreads by saliva: 'the kissing disease'.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has had 3 weeks of fatigue, fever and sore throat. He has posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen. He has no bruising, bone pain or night sweats. His temperature is 37.9°C. Investigations: blood film shows many large reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infectious mononucleosis gives a lymphocytosis with atypical (reactive) lymphocytes; leukaemia gives blasts with anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Sore throat, posterior nodes, spleen, lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infectious mononucleosis.

elim: Gives blasts, anaemia and low platelets with bruising.
Occurs in older adults with small mature lymphocytes.
Gives a neutrophilia, not atypical lymphocytes, and anterior nodes.
Can cause lymphadenopathy but rarely severe sore throat and splenomegaly.

steps.x: **C. Infectious mononucleosis.** FBC in glandular fever: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man was diagnosed with glandular fever 12 days ago. An hour ago he fell from his bicycle onto his left side. He now has left upper quadrant pain and feels faint. The abdomen is tender with guarding in the left upper quadrant. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 90/58 mmHg.

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Left upper quadrant pain and guarding over the spleen.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Splenomegaly in glandular fever makes the spleen fragile, so minor trauma can rupture it, causing LUQ pain, peritonism and haemodynamic instability.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 90/58 mmHg
steps.x: Recent glandular fever, minor trauma, LUQ peritonism, shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Splenic rupture.

elim: Epigastric pain radiating to the back, not after trauma with shock.
Loin-to-groin pain without peritonism or shock.
Epigastric pain with free air, unrelated to trauma.
Causes chest wall pain but not peritonism and shock alone.

steps.x: **E. Splenic rupture.** Glandular fever + trauma + LUQ pain + shock = splenic rupture.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman has a 1 week history of sore throat, fever and tiredness. She has exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. A heterophile antibody test is positive. She asks which germ is responsible and whether she caught it from her flatmate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV; a positive heterophile (monospot) test supports EBV, whereas CMV mononucleosis is heterophile negative.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Classic glandular fever with a positive monospot.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: EBV.

elim: Causes a similar illness but is heterophile antibody negative.
Causes gingivostomatitis and cold sores.
Causes roseola in infants.
Causes bacterial tonsillitis without splenomegaly or a positive heterophile test.

steps.x: **B. Epstein-Barr virus.** Glandular fever is caused by Epstein-Barr virus.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy has had a sore throat, fever and marked fatigue for 9 days. He has enlarged tonsils with exudate, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae. He can swallow fluids and has no breathing difficulty. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 92 bpm. His GP wants to confirm the likely diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic test?
questions.e: The monospot (heterophile antibody) test is the key first-line test for infectious mononucleosis, with EBV serology as the gold standard.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae
steps.x: Suspected glandular fever in a teenager.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Monospot (heterophile antibody) test.

elim: Not indicated in a well teenager with a viral illness.
Only if an abscess is suspected.
Does not diagnose the infection.
Detects streptococcus, not the likely cause here.

steps.x: **D. Monospot test.** Key diagnostic test: monospot; gold standard: EBV serology.

questions.stem: An 11 year old girl has had a sore throat, fever, fatigue and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy for 4 days. Her spleen is just palpable. A monospot test is negative. Her paediatrician still strongly suspects the condition and knows the monospot is often falsely negative in young children and early in the illness.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: EBV serology (such as viral capsid antigen IgM) is the gold standard and is used when the monospot is negative but suspicion remains, especially in children.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Strong suspicion but negative monospot in a child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: EBV-specific serology.

elim: Only if leukaemia is suspected from the blood count.
Far too late to guide care.
Tests for streptococcus.
Shows size but does not diagnose the cause.

steps.x: **B. EBV serology.** Monospot negative but suspicion high = EBV serology, the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman has had a sore throat, fever and fatigue for 10 days. She has posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae. A monospot test is positive. A full blood count and film are sent to help confirm the picture. She has no bruising.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the full blood count?
questions.e: The FBC typically shows a lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, which are activated CD8+ T cells; neutrophilia suggests a bacterial cause.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Confirmed glandular fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.

elim: Seen in allergy and parasitic infection.
Seen in bacterial infection.
Suggests acute leukaemia.
A reactive finding, not typical here.

steps.x: **B. Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes.** FBC in glandular fever: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes (reactive CD8+ T cells).

questions.stem: An 18 year old man with glandular fever was tackled at rugby 2 hours ago. He has left upper quadrant pain and left shoulder-tip pain. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Two large-bore cannulae are inserted and the surgical team are called.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
questions.e: Suspected splenic rupture needs an urgent group and save because of the risk of significant haemorrhage; serology and monospot do not change immediate care.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg
steps.x: Suspected splenic rupture with shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent group and save (and crossmatch).

elim: Does not show splenic injury.
The diagnosis is known and it does not change urgent care.
Do not prepare for haemorrhage.
Already diagnosed; irrelevant to bleeding.

steps.x: **E. Urgent group and save.** Suspected splenic rupture = urgent group and save given the risk of major haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has had fever, sore throat and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy for 2 weeks. A monospot test was positive. Her doctor wants a test that is more specific than the monospot and shows whether this is a recent primary infection rather than a past one.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: EBV viral capsid antigen IgM serology
questions.e: EBV serology is the gold standard; VCA IgM shows recent primary infection, whereas the heterophile antibodies of the monospot are non-specific.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Needs a specific test of recent EBV infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: EBV serology (VCA IgM).

elim: Shows atypical lymphocytes but is not specific for EBV.
Shows past CMV infection, not EBV.
Gives the same non-specific heterophile result.
Tests the wrong organism.

steps.x: **C. EBV viral capsid antigen IgM serology.** Monospot is the key first test; EBV-specific serology is the gold standard.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman has confirmed glandular fever. She has a painful sore throat and fever but can swallow fluids and soft food. She has no stridor or drooling. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. She asks what will help her feel better.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Glandular fever is self-limiting; supportive care with paracetamol or ibuprofen relieves symptoms, while antibiotics and antivirals do not help.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: can swallow fluids and soft food
what will help her feel better
steps.x: Uncomplicated glandular fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Simple analgesia and antipyretics.

elim: No benefit in a viral illness and causes a rash in EBV.
Not recommended for uncomplicated glandular fever.
Kept for severe tonsillar swelling or airway compromise.
Not indicated.

steps.x: **B. Analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen.** Supportive care with paracetamol or ibuprofen; steroids only for severe tonsillar swelling.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has had glandular fever confirmed by a positive monospot. He is eating and drinking, has no abdominal pain and his spleen is not palpable. He is worried because his flatmate said he needs antiviral tablets to get better, and asks how long he will be ill.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure that it is self-limiting and give supportive advice
questions.e: Infectious mononucleosis is generally self-limiting, so reassurance and supportive care are central; antivirals and antibiotics are not used.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Uncomplicated glandular fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reassurance and supportive care.

elim: He is eating and drinking.
Antivirals are not recommended for uncomplicated infection.
Antibiotics do not treat a viral illness.
No indication.

steps.x: **D. Reassure that it is self-limiting and give supportive advice.** Glandular fever is self-limiting: reassurance is central.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has glandular fever. Over 24 hours her tonsils have swollen so much that she can barely swallow fluids, but she has no stridor and her oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. She has been admitted for IV fluids. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
o: A short course of oral prednisolone
questions.e: Corticosteroids such as prednisolone are the second-line treatment for severe tonsillar swelling; antibiotics do not help and amoxicillin causes a rash.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: tonsils have swollen so much that she can barely swallow fluids
steps.x: Severe tonsillar swelling, not yet airway compromise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Corticosteroids, such as prednisolone.

elim: Does not reduce viral tonsillar swelling and causes a rash in EBV.
No airway obstruction at present.
No proven benefit.
Unrelated to tonsillar swelling.

steps.x: **A. A short course of oral prednisolone.** Severe tonsillar swelling in glandular fever = corticosteroids (prednisolone).

questions.stem: A 19 year old man started amoxicillin 3 days ago for a sore throat. He now has a widespread itchy pink maculopapular rash. He has posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a monospot test is positive. He took amoxicillin as a child without problems. He is breathing comfortably and has no facial swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue amoxicillin and add an antihistamine
Label him as penicillin allergic for life
Stop amoxicillin; he does not need a penicillin allergy label
questions.e: If amoxicillin has been given and the monospot is positive, stop it and manage supportively; the rash is a transient virus-related reaction, not true penicillin allergy.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Amoxicillin rash in confirmed glandular fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop amoxicillin and manage supportively.

elim: Amoxicillin is not needed for a viral illness.
There is no anaphylaxis.
The rash is a virus-related reaction, not true penicillin allergy.
No antibiotic is needed.

steps.x: **D. Stop amoxicillin; he does not need a penicillin allergy label.** Amoxicillin + EBV = rash: stop the antibiotic; it is not true penicillin allergy.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with glandular fever is seen by his GP. Since this morning he has been unable to swallow his saliva and is drooling. His voice is muffled and there is a high-pitched noise when he breathes in. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
questions.e: Stridor and drooling suggest upper airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement, which warrants urgent hospital assessment.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: high-pitched noise when he breathes in
steps.x: Stridor and drooling: threatened airway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent hospital assessment.

elim: Antibiotics do not help and delay airway care.
Unsafe with stridor.
Too slow for airway obstruction.
Unsafe with a threatened airway.

steps.x: **E. Urgent hospital assessment.** Severe sore throat or airway obstruction in glandular fever = urgent hospital assessment.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man works for a removals company carrying furniture. He has confirmed glandular fever with a palpable spleen. After 10 days he feels much better and wants to return to work and to his weekly kickboxing class. He has no abdominal pain. His pulse rate is 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Avoid alcohol for 6 months but return to all activity
Avoid contact sports for 1 week only
Avoid heavy lifting and contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
Return to all activity now he feels better
Stay on bed rest for 3 months
questions.e: NICE advises avoiding contact sports and heavy lifting for 3 to 4 weeks to reduce the risk of splenic rupture.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Glandular fever with splenomegaly and a physical job and sport.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No heavy lifting or contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks.

elim: Does not protect the spleen.
Too short; the spleen remains at risk.
Feeling better does not mean the spleen is safe.
Unnecessary; rest as needed.

steps.x: **C. Avoid heavy lifting and contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks.** NICE: avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for 3 to 4 weeks to reduce splenic rupture risk.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman has a 4 day history of sore throat, fever and marked tiredness. She has exudative tonsils, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae. Her monospot result is awaited. Her GP is considering whether to prescribe an antibiotic in case this is bacterial tonsillitis.
questions.q: Which antibiotic is most important to avoid?
questions.e: Amoxicillin or ampicillin given for an assumed bacterial sore throat causes a generalised maculopapular rash in infectious mononucleosis, so avoid them.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae
in case this is bacterial tonsillitis
steps.x: Likely glandular fever; antibiotic being considered.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Avoid amoxicillin (and ampicillin).

elim: Not linked to the characteristic rash.
Not linked to the rash, and not used for tonsillitis in this setting.
Not linked to the characteristic rash.
The usual tonsillitis choice; the classic rash is with amoxicillin or ampicillin.

steps.x: **A. Amoxicillin.** Amoxicillin or ampicillin in glandular fever gives a generalised maculopapular rash.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has glandular fever confirmed by serology. Her microbiology tutor explains that the virus belongs to a family that establishes lifelong latency after primary infection, and that it is closely related to Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (HHV-8).
questions.q: Which group does the causative virus belong to?
questions.e: EBV is a gamma-herpesvirus, like HHV-8, and infects B lymphocytes via the CD21 receptor; HSV and VZV are alpha-herpesviruses.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
A latent herpesvirus related to HHV-8.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gamma-herpesvirus.

elim: Includes HSV and varicella zoster, which are latent in neurons.
Includes CMV and HHV-6.
Includes dengue and hepatitis C.
Includes enteroviruses and hepatitis A.

steps.x: **D. Gamma-herpesvirus.** EBV = gamma-herpesvirus, infecting B cells via CD21.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man with glandular fever has marked enlargement of lymph nodes in his neck, axillae and groin, and a raised total globulin level. His immunologist explains that the virus enters a type of white cell and drives it to divide, producing many clones of that cell.
questions.q: Which best explains his lymphadenopathy and raised globulins?
questions.e: EBV infects B lymphocytes and drives polyclonal B-cell proliferation, enlarging lymphoid tissue and producing antibodies, including heterophile antibodies.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: enters a type of white cell
steps.x: EBV infects B cells and drives them to divide.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Polyclonal B-cell proliferation.

elim: Seen in allergic and parasitic disease.
Describes myeloma.
Seen in bacterial lymphadenitis.
Would not enlarge lymph nodes.

steps.x: **A. B-cell proliferation (polyclonal).** EBV infects B cells via CD21 and drives polyclonal B-cell proliferation.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman has a positive monospot test. The laboratory scientist explains that her serum caused horse red blood cells to clump together, even though she has never had contact with horses. The antibodies responsible are not directed against the virus itself.
questions.q: Which best describes the antibodies detected?
o: Autoantibodies against her own red cells
Non-specific heterophile antibodies that agglutinate animal red cells
Specific IgM against the viral capsid antigen
questions.e: The monospot detects heterophile antibodies, which are non-specific and agglutinate horse or sheep red blood cells; specific EBV antibodies are measured by serology.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: horse red blood cells to clump together
not directed against the virus itself
steps.x: Monospot detects antibodies that clump animal red cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Heterophile antibodies.

elim: These are specific EBV antibodies, detected by serology.
Would cause autoimmune haemolysis, not a positive monospot.
Cause allergy, not red cell agglutination.
This is EBV serology, not the monospot.

steps.x: **D. Non-specific heterophile antibodies that agglutinate animal red cells.** Monospot = heterophile antibodies, non-specific, agglutinating horse or sheep red cells.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with glandular fever has a spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. He plays rugby and asks why the spleen is at risk. Histology of spleens removed after rupture in this illness shows expanded white pulp packed with lymphocytes and a thin, stretched capsule.
questions.q: Which best explains why his spleen is at risk of rupture?
o: Lymphoid hyperplasia stretching a fragile capsule
questions.e: Splenomegaly results from lymphoid hyperplasia, which increases splenic fragility and predisposes to rupture with trauma or straining.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: expanded white pulp packed with lymphocytes
steps.x: Lymphocyte expansion in an enlarged spleen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lymphoid hyperplasia increasing fragility.

elim: Occurs in myelofibrosis and thalassaemia.
Seen in cirrhosis, not EBV.
A rare bacterial complication.
Causes pain but not the typical rupture mechanism.

steps.x: **B. Lymphoid hyperplasia stretching a fragile capsule.** Splenomegaly in EBV = lymphoid hyperplasia; it increases fragility, so trauma or straining can rupture it.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with glandular fever developed a widespread maculopapular rash 2 days after starting amoxicillin. A year later she is given amoxicillin for a chest infection and has no rash at all. Her GP wonders why she reacted the first time but not now.
questions.q: Which best explains the first rash?
o: Viral exanthem unrelated to the drug
questions.e: The amoxicillin rash in infectious mononucleosis is thought to be a transient, virus-related hypersensitivity reaction rather than true penicillin allergy, so it does not recur later.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Rash on amoxicillin during EBV, none on later exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A transient virus-related reaction, not true allergy.

elim: Caused by skin contact with an allergen, not an oral drug.
True allergy would recur on re-exposure.
Causes mucosal blistering and skin detachment.
The rash followed amoxicillin, which is the classic trigger in EBV.

steps.x: **A. A transient virus-related hypersensitivity reaction.** Amoxicillin rash in EBV = transient virus-related hypersensitivity, not true penicillin allergy.
